parts.title: A Virtual-Reality System Built Around a Digital Twin for Controlling a Parallel Surgical Robot, with Help from Artificial Intelligence
parts.abstract:
Robots are increasingly used in surgery that needs only small cuts, and this fast progress has created a growing need for complete systems. Such systems bring together the robot's motors, its sensors and smart control, all within one shared setup for training and for real operations. In this paper we present a virtual reality (VR) system for controlling a robot, built around a "digital twin": a virtual copy of the real robot that stays in step with it. We designed it for a new kind of surgical robot called a parallel robot, and it is meant to support both surgical training and real-time control of the robot.

We started from an ordinary VR simulator and turned it into a two-way digital twin. This lets the virtual world and the real robot stay in step with each other as things happen. The system combines the ATHENA parallel robot with a flexible laparoscopic instrument, a bendable surgical tool that gives the robot extra dexterity. ATHENA can move in 4 degrees of freedom, meaning it can move in 4 independent ways. It also follows a rule called the Remote Center of Motion (RCM): the tip of the tool always turns around a fixed point, just as a surgeon's hand does when working through a small opening in the body. Users control the robot with VR controllers, which makes it feel natural to move the robot inside an immersive virtual world.

To help users work better, we added an artificial intelligence (AI) module based on neural networks, a type of computer program that learns from examples. It works as an assistant, adjusting the robot's path in real time and guiding its movements. We ran the trained model with ONNX Runtime, a program that can read models saved in a standard format called ONNX. This makes the AI's calculations fast and lets it fit smoothly into the control system.

We tested the system in experiments, checking how well users could interact with it and carry out tasks. We also checked the robot's movements from the outside using an OptiTrack optical tracking system, which uses cameras to measure where the robot is. The results show better movement stability, faster and more efficient task completion, and better user interaction, while control stayed easy to use. Our findings highlight the potential of digital-twin VR systems as a single platform for surgical training, robot interaction and smart assistance in the next generation of medical robots.
parts.introduction_first:
Simulation has become an essential part of modern surgical training. It lets trainees repeat the same actions over and over in a safe, controlled setting, and the setting can be made as simple or as complex as the trainee's skill level. Learning surgical skills should begin in simulated settings before anyone enters the operating room, because this improves how procedures turn out and keeps patients safer [1]. Virtual reality (VR) makes it possible to build complex, interactive digital worlds where users can explore, learn and practise realistic situations under controlled conditions [2,3]. Computers have kept getting more powerful, devices have kept getting smaller, and graphics have kept getting better. Because of this, VR has grown from platforms made mainly for games into valuable tools for education, training and healthcare [4,5,6]. Earlier studies have shown that VR simulators can greatly improve surgical performance: they reduce mistakes, help people learn skills faster and make procedures more efficient. This supports bringing them into organised medical training programmes [7,8].

Besides VR simulators, several robotic platforms have played a big part in the development of robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery, which means surgery done through small cuts with the help of a robot. The da Vinci Surgical System has become the most widely used robotic platform in hospitals. It gives surgeons greater dexterity, a three-dimensional view and motion scaling, which shrinks the surgeon's hand movements into smaller, more precise ones, for complex operations [9]. Other robotic systems, including Hugo RAS, Versius and Revo-i, have been developed to make surgery more comfortable for the surgeon, easier to reach and more affordable, while keeping the same precision [10,11,12]. Parallel robots have also attracted a lot of attention. Unlike conventional serial manipulators, whose links are joined one after another like a chain, parallel robots have several arms that work together to hold a single platform. Compared with the chain-style robots, they are stiffer, place their tools more accurately and have less mass moving around.
parts.conclusion:
5. Summary and Conclusions

In this work we introduced a digital-twin system that brings together four things: immersive VR interaction, real-time in-step operation with the ATHENA parallel surgical robot, AI-assisted adjustment of the robot's path, and a separate check of the robot's movement using OptiTrack. Our design showed that these technologies can be combined in one shared surgical robotics system for interacting with the robot, training and judging how well it performs.

Ordinary VR simulators do not connect to a real robot. Our system, by contrast, keeps the virtual world and the real ATHENA robot in step as things happen. This means that commands a user makes in VR are carried out by the real robot, while the virtual copy stays in step with it. On top of that, the OptiTrack motion capture gives a separate way to check that the movements in the virtual world match the movements of the real robot.

Our experiments gave promising results for how well users could interact with the system and how efficiently they could complete tasks. However, we tested it with only a small number of participants and a simple handling task. For this reason, our findings should be seen as early evidence that the approach can work, not as firm proof that it improves performance.

In future work we will focus on larger experiments and on surgical tasks that are closer to real operations. We will also look at more advanced measures of how the robot performs while moving, how smooth its paths are, how accurately it places its tool, how much work it puts on the user, and better ways to keep the digital twin in step with the real robot. We will also explore adding advanced sensors and smarter assistance methods to make digital-twin surgical robot systems even more effective.
parts.introduction_rest:
Beyond building robotic platforms and ordinary VR training worlds, recent research has turned more and more to digital twins. A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real robot that can send information both ways: from the real robot to the virtual copy, and from the virtual copy back to the real robot. Digital twins have already worked well in many areas. These include manufacturing, robots that help people recover after injury, automated factories, medical robots and surgical training. In these settings they make it possible to watch a robot as it works, to run simulations, to predict when parts will need repair, to control the robot intelligently and to operate it from a distance. Other researchers have already described two-way digital twins that keep the virtual and real systems in step as things happen [13,14]. These systems showed the benefits of a constant flow of information between the virtual and real worlds. They made monitoring better, gave people a clearer picture of what was happening, made training more effective and helped people make decisions based on data.

A lot of progress has been made. Even so, only a few studies have brought all of these pieces together in one system designed specifically for surgical robots. Those pieces are immersive VR interaction, a digital twin that stays in step with the real robot, AI-assisted control, the real robot actually carrying out the movements, and a separate check of the robot's movement. Most earlier studies looked at just one piece at a time, such as VR training, digital-twin monitoring and in-step operation, AI-based prediction, or robot control. So there is still a need for a single platform that can do four things at once: let users interact with the robot in a natural way, keep the virtual and real systems in step in real time, give intelligent help, and measure the robot's movement with numbers. Table 1 compares some well-known surgical robotic systems with our system.

To fill this gap, we built one system for a parallel surgical robot. It brings together a digital twin, immersive VR interaction, AI-assisted adjustment of the robot's path, the real robot carrying out the movements, and a separate check of the robot's movement using cameras. The virtual and real worlds can now communicate smoothly in both directions. The system also offers better training, intelligent help with decisions, accurate control of the robot and an objective way to judge how accurate the robot's movements are.

Many VR and XR systems have already been proposed for surgery. XR, or extended reality, is a wider family of technologies that includes VR and also mixed reality, where virtual objects are placed on top of the real world. Earlier work has used VR, deep learning (a powerful kind of AI) and computer vision (letting computers understand images) to find where the ATHENA surgical robot is and where it should be [15]. Other work has explored VR environments for rehabilitation, which means helping people recover after an illness or injury [16]. Still other studies have reported VR simulators for rebuilding the jaw and face [17], careful reviews of how XR is used to teach brain surgery [18], immersive interactive systems for simulating surgery [19], and free, open-source platforms that combine VR with haptic feedback, which means feeling forces through a controller, for surgery at the base of the skull [20]. Further studies have shown that VR training can help people build skills in brain surgery [21], robot-assisted liver surgery [22], practising how to reach the kidney through a needle [23], and laparoscopic training [24]. Taken together, these works confirm that VR and XR are valuable for teaching. They improve psychomotor training, which means training the hand and eye to work together, help people understand procedures, and allow skills to be judged objectively.

Despite this progress, surgery on the pancreas is still one of the hardest kinds of surgery done through small cuts. The pancreas sits deep inside the body, close to major blood vessels and nerves, and its tissue is fragile. This means the instruments must be very steady, their movements very precise and well coordinated [25,26,27,28]. Even small technical mistakes, such as a wobbly path, a poorly placed grip or accidentally touching tissue, can lead to serious problems during and after the operation. On top of this, the surgeon works through trocars, which are small tubes pushed into the body through small cuts. Trocars limit how the instruments can move and how well the surgeon can see, which makes the job harder both mentally and technically for the surgeon [29,30]. For these reasons, organised training before the operation is especially important in robotic surgery on the pancreas.

VR training is an effective way to build the basic hand-and-eye skills needed for surgery on the pancreas through small cuts. These include placing the robot accurately, pushing the instrument in through a trocar in a controlled way, gripping tissue steadily and moving precisely in a very small working space. Tasks where the user grips and places something are especially useful. They capture the key actions in an operation, such as handling tissue, pulling it aside and placing something in the right spot, without the full complexity of a real operation. They also allow the performance to be judged objectively, using measures such as how long the task takes, how well the movements are coordinated and how steady they are [30,31,32].

Because of these needs in surgery and in teaching, we set out to build a VR system based on a digital twin for ATHENA, a new parallel surgical robot designed for surgery on the pancreas through small cuts. The real robot is built for pancreatic surgery. The virtual training world, however, is deliberately placed in a part of the body below the pancreas. There is plenty of room to work there, which makes it suitable for controlled, introductory movement tasks. This choice makes the first steps easier for new users, both mentally and technically. It lets them focus on the basic skills of interacting with the robot before moving on to situations that are more limited by the body's shape and closer to real operations.

What is new about our system is not just that it uses a two-way digital twin, because such systems have been described before. Instead, our main contribution is bringing four parts together in one system for a surgical robot. The first is immersive VR interaction, which lets users move the robot in a natural way. The second is the digital twin staying in step with the real ATHENA robot in real time. The third is an AI module that adjusts the robot's path, working with a human in the loop, meaning the human and the AI make decisions together. The fourth is a separate check of the robot's movement using an OptiTrack optical tracking system. Together, these parts give a complete system for surgical training, for interacting with the robot and for judging how well it performs.

So our main contribution goes beyond building a VR simulator. It is about combining interactive training, the virtual and real robot staying in step in real time, AI-assisted control and an outside check of the robot's movement, all within a single digital-twin system for medical robots. We intend the platform for surgical trainees, for surgeons who carry out surgery on the pancreas through small cuts, and for researchers working on robotic surgical systems. By combining immersive interaction, the real robot carrying out the movements and help based on data, the system aims to support both learning skills and the development of the next generation of ways to interact with robots in surgery. It could help make operations faster, more accurate and safer for patients, and improve the quality of care.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the ATHENA parallel robot and how its parts move. Section 3 describes how our system is built. It covers the real robot, the software, the on-screen controls, the AI module, the VR world, and how we sense the robot's movements and check them. Section 4 presents our experimental results and discusses them. Finally, Section 5 sums up our main conclusions and suggests directions for future research.
parts.methods:
3. Materials and Methods

3.1. How the System Is Built

Figure 2 shows how our system is put together. It is built around a digital twin, and it shows the two-way link between the real ATHENA parallel robot and its virtual copy. The system has two main parts. The physical part is the robot itself. The digital-twin part is a virtual world that users can step into, which we built in a virtual reality (VR) environment.

In the digital-twin part, the virtual world is an interactive picture of the robot. The user moves the virtual robot with VR controllers, and these movements are turned into motion commands. The commands are sent to the robot controller, and the real robot carries them out. So the main way of controlling the robot is through the user's actions in VR, which makes the robot easy and immersive to operate. In the physical part, the ATHENA robot's motors and joints carry out the commands under the watch of the robot controller. The robot's movements are then shown in the digital twin, because control and movement data keep flowing between the two. This keeps the virtual and real systems in step as things happen.

To check the robot from the outside, we used an OptiTrack optical tracking system (NaturalPoint Inc. 3658 SW Deschutes St, Corvallis, OR, USA). It uses cameras and small reflective markers attached to the robot to measure, separately, where the robot is and which way it is pointing. We used it to check and judge the robot's accuracy, as a reference measurement of its movement that does not affect how the digital twin is controlled.

We also built an AI-assisted control module into the system as an optional part. It can be switched on to make the robot's movements smoother and to help plan its path when needed. Even so, the main control always comes from the user through VR, and the AI module is an extra layer that improves performance. Overall, the system works in both directions. The digital twin makes the robot easy to control, the real robot carries out the matching movements in real time, and the outside tracking system checks the movements and judges how accurate the system is.

Figure 3 shows how the main parts of the system connect, and how data flows between the virtual world, the control program and the real ATHENA robot. The design is centred on the links between the user, the VR system and the robot control layer, so that users can move the robot naturally and the robot can carry out those movements in real time. The user works with the system through VR controllers and a head-mounted display, which give an immersive way to move the virtual robot inside the virtual world built in Unity, a popular game and simulation software. The VR program sends and receives data both ways with a C# program, which acts as a central hub for handling data, communication and coordination between the parts of the system.

The C# program sends the motion commands made in the virtual world to the robot controller, which carries them out through the motors of the ATHENA parallel robot. At the same time, the program runs the on-screen display on an outside monitor, showing the state of the system, the robot's measurements and how the task is going. It also collects and stores data about the user's actions and the robot's movements, and these data are used to build the examples the AI learns from. The trained neural network is saved in ONNX format and then loaded into the system with ONNX Runtime 1.2.1 (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). This lets the AI make its calculations quickly, directly inside the C# program.

The AI module is optional. When it is switched on, it fine-tunes the robot's path and helps guide its movements. The main control of the robot, however, always comes from the user through VR, which keeps the interaction natural and flexible. The OptiTrack cameras and reflective markers measure where the real robot is and which way it is pointing. This tracking system is used only to check and judge accuracy, and it does not directly affect how the system is controlled.

Figure 4 shows the experimental model of ATHENA. The active instrument, labelled (1) in Figure 4a, is mounted on the end-effector, the part of the robot that holds the tool. It lets the tool be pushed in and turned in a controlled way, so the tissue can be handled precisely during surgery. The passive spherical mechanism, labelled (2) in Figure 4a, is a set of joints that move freely without motors. It keeps the tip of the tool turning around a fixed point (the Remote Center of Motion, or RCM) and lets the point where the tool enters the body be adjusted to suit each patient.

The robot's movements are made by stepper motors, labelled (3) in Figure 4b. These are motors that move in exact, small steps. They are connected to a linear guide system, labelled (4) in Figure 4b, which moves the robot's joints accurately along straight lines. The motors are driven by B&R motor drivers (B&R Industrial Automation GmbH, Eggelsberg, Austria), labelled (5) in Figure 4c, which carry out the motion commands from the central control unit. Industrial connectors and terminal blocks, labelled (6) in Figure 4c, handle the electrical wiring and make sure signals and power are passed on reliably.

Besides these connections, how quickly the system responds also affects how well the digital twin works in real time. The response depends on several parts: reading the VR controllers, communication between the Unity virtual world (Unity 3D, version 2022.3.4f1, Unity Technologies, San Francisco, CA, USA) and the C# program, the AI's calculations, the Ethernet connection to the robot controller, how fast the motors respond, and how well the digital twin and the real robot stay in step. We did not measure the total delay from start to finish as a separate measure of performance in this study. Still, we saw no noticeable delays that affected the tasks or the user's interaction during the experiments. In future work, we will measure this total delay, the communication delays, how often the digital twin is updated, how fast the controller responds, how much the AI adds to the delay, and how often the system updates. This will let us judge in numbers how well the system works in real time.

The control system is centred on a programmable logic controller (PLC), labelled (7) in Figure 4c. A PLC is a small, rugged computer that runs the robot's control program. Ours has extra modules that can be added, and it coordinates the robot's real-time operation and the communication between all the parts. A dedicated 24 V power supply, labelled (8) in Figure 4c, keeps the control parts running steadily, and an automatic circuit breaker, labelled (9) in Figure 4c, protects against electrical faults. A Raspberry Pi 5, a small computer, labelled (10) in Figure 4c, works alongside the PLC to read sensors, connect extra devices and handle smaller control jobs. Finally, a unit that converts 230 V to 24 V, labelled (11) in Figure 4c, powers the whole system, so the experimental ATHENA platform runs safely and in a standard way.

3.2. How the Software Is Designed

The software of our system is designed to support the digital twin, so that the virtual world, the control program and the real ATHENA robot can interact in real time. It joins a VR program built in Unity with a C# control program into one platform for user interaction, data handling and robot control. The software passes information in both directions between the virtual and physical parts, so the user can work with the digital twin while the real robot carries out the matching commands. At the same time, the system collects and displays data and can also use the optional AI to process them. This supports both real-time operation and using data to improve performance.

Figure 5 shows how the software's parts fit together, using a use case diagram [36]. A use case diagram is a picture that shows who or what uses a system and what each of them does. Ours was drawn with the Unified Modeling Language [37], a standard way of drawing such diagrams. It shows how the desktop C# program, the Unity VR world, the outside control, the ATHENA parallel robot and the AI parts interact. In total, the diagram has 14 use cases, which describe the system's main jobs. Eight of them belong to the C# program and six to the Unity VR program. Together they cover choosing data, making predictions with AI, communication between the software parts, controlling the ATHENA robot and displaying information.

Four main actors, meaning the people or things that use the system, are identified. They are the human user who runs the software, the ATHENA parallel robot, the trained AI model, which we built in Python 3.12 (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA), and the Varjo XR-4 controller (Varjo Technologies Oy, Vuorikatu 20, 00100 Helsinki, Finland), which gives the user's input inside the virtual world. Nine links show how the actors connect to the C# software system [38]. Five more links show how the use cases depend on one another in logic and function. The diagram therefore shows how user interaction, the digital twin and smart control are brought together in one system.

3.3. The On-Screen Display

The graphical user interface (GUI), the on-screen display that users work with, is the layer where people and the robot meet in our digital-twin system. It has two parts that work together: an immersive VR display and a display on an ordinary desktop computer. Together they let users control, watch and collect data from the parallel surgical robot in real time, as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

The main way of controlling the robot is through the VR display. There, the user works with the digital twin of the ATHENA robot using VR controllers (Varjo XR-4). Inside this immersive world, the user moves the virtual robot directly. These movements become motion commands that are sent in real time to the control program and then carried out by the real robot.

Besides controlling movement, the VR world has interactive virtual panels that let the user reach the system's features, including switching on and setting up the AI module. The user moves a virtual laser pointer with the handheld VR controllers, which makes it easy to switch on the AI-assisted control modes for the robot's handling tasks. In this way, the user can switch on real-time path fine-tuning and movement help while the robot is working. Once a mode is chosen, the matching AI module is switched on to fine-tune the path and guide the robot's movements. The VR display therefore lets the user:

control the robot directly by moving the digital twin;

work naturally with virtual control elements;

see the robot's task and workspace in real time.

In this way, the VR display is the main way of controlling the robot, and it directly affects how the real robot behaves.

The robot control display on the desktop computer lets users watch and oversee the commands made in VR. With it, the user can manage how the system runs and check that the robot's tasks are being carried out, while the virtual and real systems stay in step.

The display has features for starting the system, overseeing commands and judging tasks, as shown in Figure 6. Besides watching, it has a set of control commands that let the user work directly with the real ATHENA robot, so that the system runs properly and safely. These commands include:

Connection control: a command that sets up communication between the control program and the real robot, so the VR world and the robot stay in step in real time.

Homing procedure: a way to start the robot by setting it to a fixed reference position, so every run begins from the same starting point.

System activation: a command that starts the robot, so the real robot follows the movements made in the virtual world.

Emergency stop mechanism: a safety feature that stops the real robot at once if it behaves unexpectedly or an emergency happens.

Figure 6

User display: robot control.

These control features make sure the robot starts reliably, runs properly and works safely, while the digital twin and the real robot stay in step. The display also shows in real time the state of the system and the details of how the task is going. These include the motor settings of the robot, where the surgical instrument is in space, the state of the end-effector (for example, whether the forceps are open or closed), feedback about contact (such as detecting when the tool touches an object), and how the task is going, including measures of performance.

Figure 7 shows the VR menu for choosing features, which lets the user switch on and set up the AI-assisted control modes.

The AI display lets users both collect data and work with the AI-assisted control module. Through it, the data from the VR controllers (Varjo XR-4) that are used to run the robot are shown and saved for later processing. The saved data include the user's control inputs and the robot's measurements, as shown in Figure 8. These include the motor settings of the parallel robot (q1, q2, q3), which describe how the robot's structure moves; the position (X, Y) of the flexible surgical instrument in space; the turning of the surgical instrument; the state of the end-effector, including whether the surgical forceps are opening and closing; and the position (X, Y, Z) of a reference point on the end-effector.

The trained models are loaded into the system with ONNX Runtime, as described in Section 3.1. When the AI module is switched on, it uses these models to fine-tune the robot's path and help guide its movements. The AI works as an optional support layer, though, and the main control always comes from the user through VR.

3.4. How We Used Artificial Intelligence to Estimate the Parallel Robot's Position

To correct the robot's path, keep its movements steady and make it better at grasping and placing the cubes, our system includes AI methods that can help the user in real time.

The AI models learn from a dataset of numbers. It has 17 input variables, which are the measurements the models are given, and 8 output variables, which are the answers the models produce. Three of the inputs, (q_1), (q_2) and (q_3), are the motor settings of the parallel robot. They move the robot's platform both sideways and up and down. They describe the robot's internal movement state and are used both for manual control and as inputs to the neural networks.

Two inputs, (f_x) and (f_y), describe the flexible tube and let the surgical forceps move sideways and from side to side. The input (r_f) describes how the surgical instrument must be turned to grip and handle objects. Two more inputs, (s_1) and (s_2), are the opening and closing angles of the first and second branches of the surgical forceps, and together they describe how firmly the instrument is gripping. Three more inputs, (t_x), (t_y) and (t_z), give the position of the centre point of the surgical forceps along the x-, y- and z-axes. They describe where the point that touches the virtual objects is in space.

The outputs we wanted the models to produce are helpful correction commands that make the robot's handling more accurate while the task is being done. We took their values from successful paths recorded while a person was doing the task. They show the adjustments needed to grip objects steadily and place them accurately.

In more detail, (o_q_1), (o_q_2) and (o_q_3) are corrections for the moving joints of the parallel robot. (o_f_x) and (o_f_y) are corrections for the position of the flexible instrument, (o_r_f) is a correction for turning the forceps, and (o_s_1) and (o_s_2) are improved commands for opening and closing the forceps. Together, these outputs make up the smallest set of control commands needed to fine-tune the path and help the robot handle objects.

The inputs for the cubes are yes-or-no (logical) variables. (b_v), (r_v) and (y_v) show whether the blue, red and yellow cubes are being gripped, and (b_c), (r_c) and (y_c) show whether each cube has been placed correctly in its target area. The first three are 1 when the cube is gripped and 0 otherwise. The last three are 1 when the cube is placed correctly and 0 otherwise. Table 2 shows the structure and meaning of all 17 input variables.

The 8 output variables, (o_q_1), (o_q_2), (o_q_3), (o_f_x), (o_f_y), (o_r_f), (o_s_1) and (o_s_2), are helpful commands that support the user while the three cubes are gripped and placed. The models produce these commands from patterns they learned during training, and the commands include corrections for the parallel robot, the flexible tube and the surgical instrument. So the outputs let the robot correct its path in real time, adjust its position in space, and improve how it turns and grips.

Our problem is a multivariate regression problem. This means the model has to predict several numbers at once from other numbers. Because of this, and because of how the dataset is built, we chose five Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) designs and three Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) designs to test and compare. An MLP is a simple kind of neural network made of layers of small calculating units, called neurons, that pass information forward. An LSTM is a kind of neural network built to remember information from earlier steps in a sequence. We chose these models because they differ in how complex they are and in how well they can handle new data they have not seen before.

3.4.1. Collecting and Checking the Data

We collected the data for training the neural networks by repeating a standard grasp-and-place task many times inside the digital twin. Each time, the person moved the virtual ATHENA robot with the Varjo XR-4 controllers, and the system kept recording the robot's state, the instrument's measurements, the positions in space and the state of the objects. This produced matching records of the 17 input variables described in Table 2. In total, we collected 2000 valid samples from many runs of the task.

Before training, we checked the dataset. We made sure the signals were lined up in time, looked at the range of values, found missing values, removed repeated samples and checked that the cube variables made logical sense. We threw away records with incomplete information or with impossible changes of state. After this check, we rescaled every variable to lie between 0 and 1, so that the numbers would stay stable while the neural networks learned. We then split the dataset into a training part and a validation part. The training part is used to teach the models, and the validation part is held back to test them on data they have not seen. We tested the models with 4-fold cross-validation, which means we split the data into four equal parts, trained on three and tested on the fourth, and repeated this so that each part was used once for testing.

3.4.2. The Machine Learning Methods We Used

Dense Multilayer Perceptron (DenseMLP) is a simple neural network in which every neuron in one layer is connected to every neuron in the next, and information flows only forward. We used it as a baseline, a starting point for judging how well the other models do at predicting several numbers at once [39]. Dropout Multilayer Perceptron (DropoutMLP) adds dropout to the DenseMLP design. Dropout randomly switches off some neurons during training, which aims to stop the model from simply memorising the training data (overfitting) and helps it work well on new data [40]. Batch Normalization Multilayer Perceptron (BatchNormMLP) adds batch normalization between the layers. This keeps the numbers flowing through the network in a steady range, which helps training run smoothly and reach a good answer faster [41]. Deep Multilayer Perceptron (DeepMLP) has more hidden layers, which helps it capture complicated, curved relationships between the inputs and outputs [42]. Wide Multilayer Perceptron (WideMLP) has more neurons in each layer instead of more layers, so it can represent more complex patterns through width rather than depth [43].

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks are designed to choose what to keep and what to forget from a sequence of data over time. This makes them good at learning links that stretch over many steps in a sequence [44]. The standard LSTM design, which we call Vanilla LSTM, has a single LSTM layer and is used to model basic links over time in the data [45]. Stacked LSTM has several LSTM layers placed one after another, which lets the model learn layered patterns and more complicated links over time [46]. Bidirectional LSTM reads the data both forwards and backwards, so it can take into account both earlier and later parts of the sequence [47].

We tuned all eight neural network designs by adjusting their hyperparameters. These are settings chosen before training, such as how many layers a network has or how big each layer is. Table 3 lists the best values we found for each design.

We did the tuning with Optuna [48], a tool that automatically tries out combinations of settings within ranges we set in advance. We chose the final settings of each model as the ones with the smallest error on the validation data, to balance accurate predictions with the ability to handle new data. The settings reflect the particular structure of each design. The deeper or wider MLP versions needed different learning rates (how big a step the model takes each time it adjusts itself), numbers of layers and training epochs (full passes through the training data) from the LSTM-based models.

Because our problem is a multivariate regression problem, we judged the eight neural networks and the combined ensemble with four measures [49]. The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is the average size of the errors, ignoring whether a prediction was too high or too low. The Median Absolute Error (MdAE) is the middle value of the error sizes, so it is less affected by a few unusual values. The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) squares each error, averages them and takes the square root, so it gives extra weight to large mistakes. The coefficient of determination (R2) shows how much of the variation in the data the model explains, where 1 would mean a perfect match. Together, these measures give a full picture of how well the models predict: the average error, how well the model copes with unusual values, how much it is penalised for large errors, and how much of the variation it explains.

We split the dataset into 75% for training and 25% for validation, which gave 1500 and 500 samples out of the 2000 records available for each variable. We also used 4-fold cross-validation, to make the results less dependent on one particular split of the data. This makes the performance numbers we report more reliable and supports the fairness of our comparison.

The measures show that the DeepMLP and Vanilla LSTM models did best on their own. The MLP-based networks showed bigger gaps between their training and validation results, which means they were more sensitive to overfitting. The LSTM-based designs behaved more steadily and handled new data better.

Table 4 lists the values of the measures for both the training and validation parts. Based on these results, we proposed an Average Voting Ensemble [50], shown in Figure 9, which combines the predictions of the DeepMLP and Vanilla LSTM networks.

We first prepared the dataset and ran 4-fold cross-validation on it, and then split it into training and validation parts. We got the final prediction by averaging the outputs of the two models. This works because the two models complement each other: the DeepMLP is good at capturing curved, complicated relationships, while the Vanilla LSTM is steady over time. The Vanilla LSTM's contribution was especially important in shrinking the gap between training and validation results, so it helped keep the ensemble from overfitting.

We took several steps to lower the risk of overfitting. First, we split the dataset into separate training (75%) and validation (25%) parts. Second, we used 4-fold cross-validation, so the results would not depend on one single split. Third, we tested designs built to avoid overfitting, such as DropoutMLP and BatchNormMLP, when choosing models. Finally, our Average Voting Ensemble combined the DeepMLP and Vanilla LSTM models, which made the validation results steadier and shrank the gap between training and validation performance.

The validation results in Table 4 show only a small gap between the training and validation measures for the final ensemble. Its R2 was 0.99693 for training and 0.98801 for validation. This shows that the ensemble handled new data well within the dataset we studied, with no sign of serious overfitting. Even so, in future studies we will consider further testing with larger groups of participants and more complex surgical situations, to judge more fully how robust the model is.

The results on the validation data confirm that our ensemble predicts better than any single neural network. It has the lowest validation errors (MAE = 0.02284, RMSE = 0.03159) and the highest R2 (0.98801).

These results show that combining designs that complement each other improves overall prediction accuracy. The smaller gap between the training and validation measures also shows that the model behaves steadily and does not overfit in a serious way. The ensemble keeps the DeepMLP's strength at representing complicated patterns while gaining the steadier handling of new data from the Vanilla LSTM. So combining the DeepMLP and Vanilla LSTM neural networks in this voting ensemble shows high potential to give precise and reliable help with positioning and handling objects in parallel robots.

3.5. Building the Virtual Reality Program

The VR program is the main place where users interact with our digital-twin system. It lets them control the ATHENA parallel surgical robot naturally, see what is happening in real time and carry out tasks. We built the virtual world in Unity using the ProBuilder package [51,52], which let us quickly build and improve the workspace without needing separate modelling software. To give a realistic surgical setting, we made a virtual patient model with MakeHuman [53] and added a skeleton and internal organs, as shown in Figure 10.

The robot's structure and the surgical instrument are the main parts of the digital twin. We designed them in Siemens NX, a 3D design program, where we modelled and checked the robot's structure, its degrees of freedom, the limits on its movement and its gripper. We then exported the finished design to Unity, so that the virtual and real systems matched while the user could still interact with the robot in real time. Figure 10d shows the main parts built into the VR world.

In the VR program, the user works with the digital twin using Varjo XR-4 controllers. The controller movements are matched to the matching movements of the virtual robot, and these become commands that are sent to the control program and then carried out by the real robot. This creates a real-time loop between the user's actions, the virtual robot's movement and the real robot's actions, as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

The program supports handling tasks, such as gripping and placing objects with the surgical instrument, so that both the user's actions and the robot's performance can be judged. While the task is being done, the user controls where the instrument is, which way it points and the state of the gripper, while seeing a constant visual feedback. Interactive menus and virtual control panels also let the user set up the system and switch on extra features, including the AI-assisted control module.

Besides control and display, the VR system also collects data: it records the user's inputs, which are later used to train the AI models. Overall, the VR program gives a single platform for immersive interaction, real-time robot control, simulation and improvement based on data within our digital-twin system.

3.6. Using the Virtual World

Surgical robots and special simulators have drawn a lot of attention because they can make operations more accurate, lower the risks during surgery and help train medical staff well. In the simulator, the user can learn to use the surgical robot by practising with a surgical forceps that handles various objects, such as three cubes. To control the surgical robot in the VR program, the user uses two controllers (Figure 11b). These let the user interact with the robot naturally and precisely, which helps them position the robot and carry out different simulated surgical operations.

With the controllers, the user can position the robot to do the following actions:

Start position (Figure 12a): the robot's starting position, where the simulation begins;

Position 1 (Figure 12b): reached by sliding the slider on the controller along the −X axis (Figure 11b, (1));

Position 2 (Figure 12c): reached by sliding the slider on the controller along the +X axis (Figure 11b, (1));

Position 3 (Figure 12d): reached by sliding the slider on the controller along the +Y axis (Figure 11b, (1));

Position 4 (Figure 12e): reached by sliding the slider on the controller along the −Y axis (Figure 11b, (1));

Pushing the surgical instrument in and pulling it out (Figure 12f): done by pressing two special buttons (Figure 11b, (2));

Opening and closing the surgical forceps (Figure 12g): opening is started by pressing the button (Figure 11b, (7)) and closing by pressing the button (Figure 11b, (8));

Turning the surgical forceps a full 360° (Figure 12h): done by pressing two buttons in turn (Figure 11b, (6));

Position 1 of the surgical forceps (Figure 12i): reached by bending the flexible tube along the −X axis (Figure 11b, (5));

Position 2 of the surgical forceps (Figure 12j): reached by bending the flexible tube along the +X axis (Figure 11b, (5));

Position 3 of the surgical forceps (Figure 12k): reached by bending the flexible tube along the −Y axis (Figure 11b, (5));

Position 4 of the surgical forceps (Figure 12l): reached by bending the flexible tube along the +Y axis (Figure 11b, (5)).

We chose the cube-handling task on purpose as a simple test scenario, not as a direct copy of pancreatic surgery. Its main aim was to test the basic hand and eye skills needed in robotic surgery through small cuts. These include placing the instrument precisely, gripping in a controlled way, coordinating the hands and eyes, planning the path and moving objects towards a target. The task also gives a controlled setting that can be repeated, for judging how users interact with the system, how well the AI guides them and how well the digital twin stays in step.

The task captures several key parts of handling objects with a robot, but it does not copy the full complexity of real surgery. That includes tissue changing shape, forces acting on the tissue, differences between patients' bodies, bleeding, poor visibility and other factors that matter in real operations. So our experimental scenario should be seen as a first check of our system, not as a complete surgical simulation. In future work, we will extend the digital twin towards realistic surgical situations that include tissue models that change shape, tasks specific to particular procedures and training methods that match real clinical practice.

3.7. How We Ran the Experiments

We recruited six participants who already had experience using VR. Each participant did the same object-handling task under two conditions:

Ordinary VR control without AI help;

VR control with AI help to fine-tune the robot's path.

In the task, the participant gripped three coloured cubes and placed them in set target spots. For each trial, we recorded how long the task took, the robot's path and the system's measurements. Every participant did the steps in the same order. Before the experiments, we gave a short practice session so that participants would be familiar with the system and so that learning would affect the results as little as possible. During the experiments, we asked the participants to finish the task as quickly and accurately as they could.

3.8. How We Checked the Robot's Movements

We measured the real robot's movements separately with an OptiTrack optical tracking system. It had several infrared cameras and reflective markers attached to the robot's structure. We calibrated the system, which means we lined up the coordinate systems of the Unity virtual world, the robot controller and the OptiTrack measuring system so that they all used the same reference points and directions.

For each point we sampled, we calculated the straight-line (Euclidean) distance between the reference position from the digital twin and the matching position measured by OptiTrack. From these errors, we calculated the average position error, the root mean square error (RMSE) and the largest error.

We used these measures to show how closely the digital twin matched the real robot.

4. Results and Discussion

4.1. Checking That the Virtual Copy Stays in Step with the Real Robot

Adding VR to the training of robotic surgery brings clear benefits. It can improve technical performance, shorten the time needed to finish a task, and let people learn skills safely in a controlled simulation [54]. In our simulator, the user carries out an organised training task that copies the key steps of surgery done through small cuts with a robot. First, the user has to place the ATHENA robot so that the surgical tool can be pushed through a trocar. A trocar is a small opening in the surface of the virtual patient, and Figure 13a,b shows it.

To help users judge where things are in space, they can switch on a see-through view with the VR controller. This lets them see the body's inner structures, as Figure 13c shows. Once the tool is in place, the user does a "grasp and place" task. Using the surgical forceps, they pick up three coloured cubes one after another and put each one in its own target area, as Figure 13d,e shows. The task tests how well the user coordinates their movements, how precise they are and how steady they keep the motion. The system records how long the task takes automatically, from the moment the robot is correctly placed until all the cubes have been put in place.

Our system also carries VR interaction over to the real ATHENA robot, which is the physical partner of the digital twin. Movement commands made in VR are sent to the robot's control system, and the real robot carries them out. This keeps the virtual and real worlds working in step. Users can also switch on an optional AI module based on a neural network. It gives guidance on the robot's path while the tool is being pushed in and objects are being moved. The module does not take over from the user. Instead, it helps keep the motion steady, the placement accurate and the task efficient.

To check the system from the outside, we used an OptiTrack motion capture system to measure how the real ATHENA robot actually moved, as Figure 13f shows. We attached reflective markers to key parts of the robot and to the area around the trocar. These markers let the system work out where the robot was, and which way it was facing, as the task was carried out. The motion capture system was not part of the real-time control loop, the chain of signals that runs the robot. We used it only as a separate reference, to see how well the commands made in VR matched the robot's real movement.

To measure this match, we compared the path recorded in the digital twin, which runs in Unity (a widely used program for building virtual worlds), with the path measured by OptiTrack. Before working out any errors, we lined up the two sets of data in time. We also put them both into the same coordinate frame, which is simply a shared set of directions for measuring positions. To do this, we used the known position of the trocar and the starting position of the tool, which we had calibrated, meaning carefully measured and set. Then, at each point in time, we calculated the position error. This is the straight-line distance, called the Euclidean distance, between the point the VR world commanded and the matching point measured on the real robot.

To put a number on how well the digital twin and the real robot matched, we compared the path made in the Unity virtual world with the path measured separately by OptiTrack. Before the analysis, we lined up both sets of data in time and converted them into the same coordinate frame, using the calibrated trocar position and the robot's starting position. We then calculated the position error for each point in time as the straight-line distance between the virtual point and the matching OptiTrack measurement:

(5) e_i = √[(x_i^VR − x_i^Opt)² + (y_i^VR − y_i^Opt)² + (z_i^VR − z_i^Opt)²]

Here x, y and z are the three directions of space, and the small i stands for each point in time.

From the full series of errors, we then calculated the summary numbers shown in Figure 14. The mean error is simply the average of all the position errors. The root mean square error (RMSE) is a kind of average that gives extra weight to large mistakes, so it is a little bigger than the plain average. We calculated it as:

(6) RMSE = √[(1/N) ∑_{i=1}^{N} e_i²]

In this formula, N is the number of points in time, and the ∑ sign means "add up all of them". The maximum error is the largest gap we recorded between the virtual and real paths.

For the example path shown in Figure 14, the real robot followed the movement made in VR with only small differences. The mean position error was 2.42 mm, the root mean square error was 2.56 mm, and the maximum error was 4.68 mm. The biggest differences happened mostly when the robot changed direction. At those moments, small delays between the VR command and the robot's response became easier to see.

These errors may come from several sources. There may be a small delay in passing messages between the computer and the robot. The robot's parts may bend slightly under load. The coordinate frames of OptiTrack and the digital twin may not line up perfectly. And both the motors and the tracking system can only measure and move in limited steps. Even so, the small differences support the idea that VR can be used as an easy-to-use way to control the real ATHENA robot. They also strengthen the case that our digital-twin design works.

The mean tracking error of 2.42 mm also shows that, under the conditions of our experiments, the path made in the digital twin closely matched the movement of the real ATHENA robot. Still, this number should not be taken as firm proof that the system is ready for surgery. How small a positioning error is acceptable in surgery through small cuts depends on the particular procedure, the body parts involved, the size of the tools and the safety margins.

So the accuracy we report should mainly be seen as evidence that the virtual and real parts of our system stay in step well. Our results confirm that the digital twin can keep the VR commands and the real robot's movement in a consistent match while a task is carried out. However, before anyone could consider using the system in surgery, more studies will be needed. These would use realistic surgical phantoms, which are models of the body built to behave like real tissue. They would also include how the tool pushes into tissue, force feedback (feeling how hard the tool is pressing), and paths like those found in real operations.

4.2. Testing the System in Experiments

To see how the AI module affects the way a task is carried out, we ran a first experiment using the VR-based digital twin described in Section 4.1. Our aim was to find out whether AI-assisted control helps users work more efficiently when they move the robot. We chose the pick-and-place task on purpose as a simple first test of handling. It is simpler than real laparoscopic procedures such as stitching, passing a needle or handling tissue. But it still lets us measure, in a fair and repeatable way, how accurately the robot places its tool, how well it grasps objects, how steady its path is and how well the user interacts with it. In future studies, we will move on to more realistic training tasks for surgery through small cuts.

This first study of how easy the system is to use involved six participants. They all had engineering backgrounds and had worked with robots and virtual reality systems before. The study was not meant to test the system in surgery. Instead, it looked at how users interact with the digital twin, how well they control the robot and whether the system can work at all. For this reason, the results should be read as an early engineering check, not as a study of surgery. Before taking part, every participant gave informed consent, meaning they agreed to join after being told what the study involved.

Each participant did the same standard grasp-and-place task described in Section 4.1, twice. The first time, they controlled the robot by hand through the VR interface, with no AI help. The second time, they used the same VR control with the AI module switched on. In both cases, the task meant placing the robot, pushing the surgical tool through the trocar, and then picking up three coloured objects one after another and putting each in its own target area. We compared the two conditions using the total time each participant took to finish the task. The built-in timing system shown in Figure 6 measured this automatically.

We wanted to know whether the faster times with AI help were statistically significant. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference between the two conditions, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. To test this, we used a paired t-test. This test compares two measurements taken from the same people, here each participant's time with AI off and with AI on. Because every participant did the task in both conditions, a paired analysis was the right choice.

The average time to finish the task fell from 150.69 ± 24.22 seconds without AI help to 92.39 ± 18.82 seconds with it. The number after the ± sign shows how much the times varied between participants. On average, the task took 58.30 seconds less, which is 38.69% shorter than the time without AI help. The paired t-test showed a statistically significant improvement (t(5) = 18.52, p = 8.5 × 10⁻⁶). The p-value tells us that if AI help really made no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance less than 1 time in about a million.

We also calculated the effect size, which shows how big a difference is compared with the normal spread in people's times. Ours was extremely large (Cohen's d = 7.56), which points to a substantial practical effect of the AI guidance. Together, these results show that our AI-assisted digital twin makes the task much more efficient, while the user still controls the robot.

Figure 15 shows the results, comparing each participant's time in the two conditions. Every participant finished the task faster with AI help than by hand without it. This may be because the AI module can give smoother and steadier control signals, especially during key moments such as pushing the tool in and placing objects. By fine-tuning the commands the user makes, the AI-assisted mode reduces sudden jerks in movement and makes it easier to handle the surgical tool precisely.

We want to stress that the AI module is an optional helper and does not replace the user's control. The user still makes the movement commands through the VR interface, and the AI module only improves the quality and steadiness of those commands. Our early engineering study included only a small number of participants, so it cannot lead to conclusions about surgery. Even so, every participant finished the task faster with AI help. This suggests that AI-assisted interaction can make tasks more efficient within our digital twin system.

4.3. Discussion

Our results show that it is possible to bring together immersive VR, real-time control of a robot and AI help in one digital-twin system for surgical robots. Ordinary VR simulators do not connect to a real robot. Our approach, by contrast, links the virtual world directly to the real ATHENA robot, so it can be used both for training and for real-time control. The VR world is the main way users control the robot, and they can move it naturally through its digital twin. This way of interacting helps users judge where things are in space and keeps them engaged, both of which matter for surgical training and learning skills.

Our experiments show that the system supports carrying out handling tasks in a consistent way, in a controlled and safe setting. We chose the pick-and-place task as a first, simple test of handling, not as a copy of a real surgical procedure. Its purpose was to check the basic interaction, placement and grasping before moving on to more complex laparoscopic training tasks. Measuring the time to finish the task lets us judge, in a fair and repeatable way, how efficiently users interact with the system. The AI module also helps users perform better by guiding the robot's path and smoothing its movements, as the shorter times across all participants show. However, the AI part remains a helper and does not replace the user's control. This keeps the human-in-the-loop principle, which means a person always stays in charge, as medical robots require.

Another important part of our approach is that the real ATHENA robot carries out the actions of the digital twin. Movement commands made in VR are sent to the real robot, so the virtual and real systems work in step. The OptiTrack tracking system adds a separate layer of checking. It measures where the robot is and which way it faces without changing the control loop. This lets us judge, in a fair and repeatable way, how well the commanded movements match the ones actually carried out.

We should point out several limitations. First, we tested the system with only a small number of participants. This limits how strong the statistical results are and how widely they apply. Also, the people in this early study had engineering backgrounds and experience with robots and virtual reality, not the skills of a surgeon. Future studies should therefore include larger groups of surgical residents (doctors in training) and experienced surgeons.

Second, the pick-and-place task is a simple handling test. It is good for checking placement accuracy, grasping, path steadiness and user interaction, but it does not fully capture how complex surgery through small cuts is. In future testing, we will add tasks closer to real operations, such as stitching, passing a needle, handling tissue and cutting it apart.

Third, several sources of positioning error may affect how well the system works overall. These include small mismatches between the coordinate frames of the virtual and real systems. There may also be delays in passing messages between Unity, the C# application (the program written in the C# programming language) and the robot's controller. The robot's parts may bend slightly under load, and the parts may not fit together perfectly. The motors can only move in limited steps, and the OptiTrack tracking system has some uncertainty.

Another important direction for future research is to test the robot platform in a standard way, following internationally recognised standards for robots and medical devices. These include ISO 9283 [55] and, where it applies, IEC 80601-2-77 [56]. Such tests were beyond the scope of this study. However, our current setup has the main parts needed for a first standard check. The robot's controller lets it repeat the same path again and again. The separate OptiTrack optical tracking system measures the robot's tool tip without changing the control loop.

Still, our current results do not show that the system formally meets these standards or is ready for surgery. Future studies will therefore use standard test positions and paths to check several things. These are placement accuracy, repeatability (how closely the robot repeats the same movement), path accuracy, path repeatability, how far the path strays, how smooth the movement is and how steady the placement is. We will also measure how uncertain the OptiTrack measurements are. To do this, we will look at the leftover errors after calibration, take repeated measurements with the robot still and moving, check how well the coordinate frames line up, and, where possible, compare with other reference measuring devices. We will report this uncertainty together with the robot's performance numbers. This will show whether the measuring system is accurate and precise enough for what is needed.

The AI module has limitations too. Our AI model combined two kinds of neural network, called DeepMLP and Vanilla LSTM, and it predicted very well (R² = 0.98801). R² is a score of how well predictions match real measurements, where 1 would be a perfect match. However, the model was trained on 2000 examples collected in a controlled experiment. To make the model more reliable and able to work in more situations, we will need more examples from more users, more handling tasks and more robot setups.

Other VR-based surgical training systems have been described in earlier research. Compared with them, our system links the digital twin, the real robot, AI-assisted smoothing of the robot's path and a separate optical check of the movement more closely together. Even so, more studies comparing it with established laparoscopic simulators are needed before we can draw firm conclusions about how well it trains people.

Overall, our system is a step towards bringing together immersive interaction, AI-assisted control and real robot movement within a digital twin. Combining VR control, a separate check of the robot's movement and help based on data gives a promising starting point for future training environments that adapt to the user, and for smart robots used in medicine.

4.4. Statistical Analysis and Study Limitations

To look more closely at our experimental findings, we summarised the task completion times with basic statistics. We focused on comparing the overall patterns of performance with ordinary control and with AI-assisted control. Our main aim was to find out whether AI help could be added to our digital twin system, so we chose the time to finish the task as the main measure of performance.

Because this early study included only six participants, the results should be seen as a first check of whether the approach can work, not as firm proof that it performs better. The AI-assisted condition was linked to shorter times, but with so few people we cannot draw strong statistical conclusions about a general improvement in performance.

Even so, the results suggest that our AI-assisted digital twin could make interaction more efficient while keeping the human in control. Future studies will include more participants and a wider range of measures. These will include how smooth the path is, how efficient the path is, placement accuracy, how repeatable the movement is, the delay in keeping the virtual and real systems in step, how much work the task puts on the user, and how users feel about the experience. Such analyses will allow a fuller statistical check of our approach.
